We establish an evaluation protocol to systematically as-
sess Mem-X. The protocol controls access to cross-episode
coordinates (Section III-A): Level 1 shares a global frame,
while Levels 2 and 3 provide only episode-local poses
and withhold inter-episode transforms, so later tasks cannot
be solved from a shared pose. Following common VLN
settings [3], [11], we report Success Rate (SR) and Success
weighted by Path Length (SPL) to measure task completion.
Because these endpoint-based metrics cannot tell whether
the agent used historical memory, we further propose metrics
for memory-related capabilities, covering target recall, cross-
episode localization, constrained completion, and historical-
route reproduction.

truly found the target object, we use Memory Recall Rate

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Headline outcomes are measured with objective simulator ground-truth coordinates and paths through MRR, Loc-SR, C-SR, C-SPL, and ST-nDTW, not by the VLM or learned components used in MemBridge.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Objective Habitat ground-truth trajectory and coordinate metrics, including MRR, Loc-SR, C-SR, C-SPL, and ST-nDTW.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Heuristic feature matching with SuperPoint/LightGlue and SE(2) RANSAC, semantic scene graph construction, and zero-shot Qwen-3.5-27B prompting without benchmark fine-tuning.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims that existing VLN agents struggle when navigation strictly depends on cross-episode memory and lack of global poses are well supported by baseline results (e.g., Level 3 C-SR near 0-7%). The claimed performance gains from MemBridge are verified across all tested architectures.
primary.evaluation_assessment: Four established VLN baselines (CMA, ETPNav, JanusVLN, Uni-LaViRA) are evaluated with and without MemBridge across objective metrics including Memory Recall Rate (MRR), Constrained Success Rate (C-SR), and Spatio-Temporal nDTW (ST-nDTW). Component ablations in Table V clearly isolate the contributions of fine retrieval, cross-episode localization, and frontier exploration.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Headline performance is evaluated directly using objective simulator ground-truth coordinates and paths rather than relying on model self-scoring.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Objective ground-truth navigation trajectory and coordinate metrics in Habitat (MRR, Loc-SR, C-SR, C-SPL, and ST-nDTW).
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Heuristic feature matching (SuperPoint/LightGlue + SE(2) RANSAC), semantic scene graph construction, and zero-shot VLM prompting (Qwen-3.5-27B) without fine-tuning on the benchmark.

primary.limitations: The authors clearly acknowledge benchmark limitations, specifically the restriction to single-floor environments in simulation and reliance on drift-free simulator ground-truth odometry.
primary.method_assessment: The benchmark protocol carefully disallows shared coordinates in Levels 2 and 3, requiring cross-episode visual self-localization, and defines strict geometric constraints for route retracing. MemBridge provides an explicit modular design combining incremental 3D semantic scene graphs, feature matching with SE(2) RANSAC for pose alignment, and two-stage coarse-to-fine VLM retrieval.
primary.quality_rationale: The benchmark addresses a clear gap in cross-episode navigation benchmarks by making memory strictly necessary rather than optional. The experimental setup is thorough, the proposed baseline is soundly constructed and ablated, and the conclusions are well-supported without overclaiming.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces Mem-X, a cross-episode vision-and-language navigation benchmark consisting of 2,071 episodes (1,204 memory-dependent) across 34 scenes with three progressive difficulty tiers requiring memory recall, in-memory localization, and off-memory route re-entry without shared global coordinate frames, accompanied by a modular baseline architecture (MemBridge).
